summary: Defines a schema for storing Java objects in an LDAP directory, so applications can look up serialized or referenced objects by name. This is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: A directory is like a phone book. This says how to file Java program pieces in it so programs can find them later.

questions: how to store java objects in ldap
how to use jndi with ldap
subtitle: A schema for storing Java program objects in an LDAP directory.

tldr.problem: Java applications need to store and retrieve objects from a central location, and LDAP directories are ideal for this, but there was no standard way to represent Java objects in LDAP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines LDAP object classes and attributes for storing three types of Java objects: serialized objects (frozen copies), marshalled objects (with codebase information), and JNDI references (pointers to objects). Each type gets its own schema element.
tldr.outcome: Java applications can now share objects through LDAP directories using a common, interoperable schema.

facts.label: Attributes defined
facts.value: 7 (javaClassName, javaClassNames, javaCodebase, javaSerializedData, javaFactory, javaReferenceAddress, javaDoc)

today: RFC 2713 is an Informational memo from October 1999 and remains the standard schema for Java objects in LDAP. It was created alongside RFC 2714 (CORBA references in LDAP) at Sun Microsystems and continues to be referenced in Java directory integration projects.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
LDAP directories traditionally store people and organizational data. For Java applications distributed across a network, the directory becomes a natural central repository for sharing Java objects. Unlike traditional use cases where you look up a person's phone number, Java applications need to look up objects representing services, configurations, or resources.

This RFC defines a common schema so any Java application can store and retrieve Java objects from an LDAP directory in an interoperable way. The schema covers four scenarios: storing serialized Java objects (a complete snapshot of an object's state), marshalled objects (serialized objects with automatic codebase information), JNDI references (pointers to objects), and remote objects accessed via Java Remote Method Invocation.
sections.eli5: Java programs running on different computers sometimes need to share objects with each other. A directory is a good place to keep them. This explains the standard way to store Java objects in a directory.

sections.title: Types of Java Objects and Their Representations
sections.content:
The schema defines four object representations. A serialized object is a byte-for-byte snapshot of a Java object created by converting its state into a stream. To use it later, the application deserializes the stream back into a copy of the object. The javaSerializedObject class stores the serialized bytes, the class name, optional ancestor class names, and optional URLs pointing to where the class definition can be loaded.

A marshalled object is like a serialized object but created using the Java RMI infrastructure, which automatically captures where the class definitions live (the "codebase"). This saves developers from having to manually set the codebase attribute. A JNDI reference is not the object itself but a set of instructions on how to create or locate it: a factory class name and one or more addresses telling the application how to reach the object. Remote objects (objects running on a remote machine that can be called via RMI) are stored either as marshalled objects or as JNDI references, not as the actual remote object.
sections.eli5: There are different ways to store Java objects. A serialized object is a complete snapshot. A marshalled object is like a snapshot but remembers where the class definitions are. A reference is just instructions on how to find the object. Remote objects are special because they are on another computer.

sections.title: Object Classes and Attributes
sections.content:
The schema defines five object classes and seven attributes. The base class javaObject is abstract and cannot exist alone; it requires a mandatory javaClassName attribute (the fully qualified Java class name like "java.lang.String"). Optional attributes include javaClassNames (ancestor classes and interfaces), javaCodebase (URLs for class definitions), javaDoc (URL to Java documentation), and description (human-readable text).

The javaContainer structural class provides a dedicated container for a Java object. The javaSerializedObject auxiliary class (mixed in with another structural class) adds a mandatory javaSerializedData attribute containing the serialized bytes. javaMarshalledObject is identical except semantically: the javaSerializedData field contains a marshalled object, which already encodes the codebase. javaNamingReference stores reference information using optional javaReferenceAddress (a sequence of address instructions) and javaFactory (the factory class name). All classes except javaContainer are auxiliary, meaning they must be mixed with a structural class like javaContainer when creating a directory entry.
sections.eli5: The schema defines the building blocks. The main block is javaObject, which says every Java object must have a class name. Then there are special types: one for serialized objects, one for marshalled objects, one for references. Each has the attributes it needs.

sections.title: Using the Schema in Practice
sections.content:
Developers store a Java object by first deciding which representation suits them. For a complete object snapshot, javaSerializedObject is simplest but requires manually setting the codebase attribute if users need to load classes from somewhere. For automatic codebase capture, create a java.rmi.MarshalledObject wrapper first, then store it as javaMarshalledObject. For objects that cannot or should not be fully stored, create a javax.naming.Reference with the factory and address information, then store it as javaNamingReference.

When retrieving, the application looks up the directory entry, determines which class to use (by checking javaClassName or searching by javaClassNames), and then either deserializes the javaSerializedData field or uses the reference information to instantiate the object. The javaCodebase attribute guides the class loader on where to fetch class definitions if they are not already available locally.
sections.eli5: To save an object, you decide how: as a complete copy, or as instructions on where to find it. To retrieve it, you look it up in the directory and then either copy it back or follow the instructions to recreate it.

sections.title: Security and Interoperability
sections.content:
Storing a serialized object in the directory makes the object's state available to anyone with directory access, outside its original runtime context. If the object contains sensitive data, it should not be stored in the directory. The RFC defers to the Java Object Serialization Specification for details on serialization security. Directory access control mechanisms (via LDAP ACLs) provide the primary protection.

The schema is compatible with multiple LDAP implementations because it uses only standard attribute syntaxes and LDAP conventions. JNDI references use human-readable formats for StringRefAddr (string addresses) and Base64 encoding for binary addresses, making them inspectable and editable by standard directory tools. This interoperability enables any Java application to read and write objects stored by any other, provided they understand the same object types and factories.
sections.eli5: Be careful when storing objects with secrets in them, because anyone with directory access will see them. The good news is that the format is standard and readable, so different programs can share objects.
